title: Summer
summary: Summer on Native Long Island centered on coastal abundance, shellfish harvesting, fishing, berry gathering, and the steady tending of gardens.
content:
Summer made Long Island's estuaries, tidal flats, bays, and fields especially important. Communities could live close to shorelines and waterways while fishing, gathering shellfish, and tending gardens. This was not a random movement across the landscape; it was informed by knowledge of tides, fish, plants, heat, winds, and soils.

Fish, crabs, clams, oysters, scallops, berries, and other foods helped support summer life. Some foods could be smoked, dried, or otherwise prepared for later use. Gardens also needed attention, including weeding, protecting young plants, and supporting corn as it grew.

Summer helps explain why shell middens, fishing places, and coastal village areas matter as educational evidence. Public interpretation should use broad examples and museum context rather than encouraging visits to vulnerable archaeological places.
